summary: A best current practice describing what the Internet community expects from Computer Security Incident Response Teams. It cannot define requirements right for every team, but it lists topics each team should state clearly, like its mission and services.

eli5.summary: When a computer is attacked, a response team helps. This memo lists what such teams should tell people about what they do.

questions: what to expect from a csirt
computer security incident response team guidelines
what should a csirt publish about itself
what is the csirt template in rfc 2350
subtitle: What the Internet community expects a security incident response team to tell its users, and a template for saying it.

tldr.problem: Users had misunderstandings about what to expect from computer security incident response teams, and teams did not consistently say who they serve or what they do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the topics a team should publish (contact details, charter, policies, services, forms, disclaimers) and gives an outline template plus a filled-in example for a fictitious team.
tldr.outcome: It sets no single set of requirements, but gives constituents a clear way to understand and compare their team. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 21).

today: RFC 2350 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 21) published in June 1998. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Teams Should Explain Themselves
sections.content:
The GRIP Working Group wrote this document to describe the community's expectations of Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). A CSIRT is a team that performs, coordinates and supports the response to security incidents that involve sites within a defined constituency. Past misunderstandings about what to expect from such teams are the reason for the document.

The RFC does not try to specify the correct answer for any topic. It describes what each topic means. Constituents should be able to expect the services a team describes in its completed template, and users need to know that they should report incidents, and how and where. Many incidents cross site boundaries, so teams must also cooperate with each other.
sections.eli5: A fire station is only useful if people know it exists, what it does and how to call it. This memo says response teams should make that clear.

sections.title: Publishing, Relationships and Secure Communication
sections.content:
The scope covers three areas. First, a team must publish its policies and procedures to its constituency; the RFC calls this mandatory. Not everything has to be public, since outsiders do not need a team's internal workings. Teams are recommended to publish on their own information server, and because users must check that a template is authentic, digital signatures are highly recommended.

Second, most incidents involve parties outside the constituency, so teams work with other CSIRTs. The RFC separates a peering agreement, where teams agree to work together and share information, from simple co-operation, where one party just asks another for help. The details are left to the teams.

Third, teams need secure communication: confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. Public keys, for PGP or PEM, must be authenticated before use, and secret keys must be exchanged in advance over a secure channel. The RFC leaves the technical problems of secure communication out of scope.
sections.eli5: A team should tell everyone how it works, who it teams up with, and how to talk safely, so no one can fake a message from it.

sections.title: The Template: Document Information, Contacts and Charter
sections.content:
The core of the RFC is a template a CSIRT fills in. It starts with document information: the date of last update, a distribution list for notifications of changes and where the current version can be found. Outdated documents can do more harm than good, and digital signatures should be used on update messages and the online copy.

Contact information covers the team name, address, time zone, telephone and fax numbers, email address, public keys and encryption information, team members and operating hours. Some teams may choose not to publish member names.

Every CSIRT must have a charter with four parts: a mission statement, a constituency, a sponsoring organization and an authority. The constituency creates a perimeter around those the team serves, and a team that withholds it should explain why. A team may or may not have authority to intervene in all systems inside its perimeter. The RFC notes that disclosing authority may expose a team to liability claims and advises seeking legal advice.
sections.eli5: The template is a form with boxes: when it was written, how to reach the team, who they help and who gave them permission to do it.

sections.title: Policies on Incidents, Disclosure and Communication
sections.content:
The policy section covers three things. The team lists the types of incidents and level of support it offers, plus a default for types not listed, and says whether it will act on vulnerability information. Acting on such information is described as an optional proactive service, not a core requirement.

The disclosure policy says who receives reports in each situation. Related groups include other CSIRTs, vendors, law-enforcement agencies and the press. Security information is usually confidential by default, but rigid secrecy makes a team look like an information 'black hole' and can reduce cooperation. Unique ticket numbers and explicit handoff procedures help teams cooperate and avoid loops. Legal constraints may require or limit disclosure.

The communication and authentication policy must describe secure and verifiable methods. The template should include public keys or pointers to them with fingerprints. As a minimum, every CSIRT should have a PGP key available if possible, and correspondence should include digital signatures. For phone or fax, a team may keep agreed secret passwords or phrases; their existence may be published but not the secrets.
sections.eli5: The team explains what kinds of trouble it handles and who it may tell about your problem. It also says how to be sure a message really came from it.

sections.title: Services, Forms and Disclaimers
sections.content:
Services fall into two groups: real-time incident response, and non-real-time proactive activities. Incident response has three parts. Triage covers report assessment and verification. Coordination covers categorizing information under the disclosure policy and notifying involved parties on a need-to-know basis. Resolution is usually optional and covers technical assistance, eradication and recovery.

Proactive services are also usually optional: information provision, security tools, education and training, product evaluation, and site security auditing and consulting.

Teams should offer incident reporting forms, ideally online, so a constituent can prepare answers before contacting the team. The template ends with a disclaimer, since the description is not a contract but could still lead to liability. A translation should carry a disclaimer and a pointer to the original.
sections.eli5: Like a doctor's clinic, the team first checks how bad the problem is, then tells the right people, and may help you get better. Some extras, like classes, are optional.

sections.title: The Outline and the XYZ-CERT Example
sections.content:
Appendix D condenses the topics into a point-form outline with seven top-level parts. Appendix E fills it in for a fictitious team called XYZ-CSIRT, described as 'XYZ University' in the text. The RFC states that the example is for illustration only and is not an endorsement by the working group or the IETF of any particular policy. Teams may use any of it, but use is not mandatory and often not appropriate.

Appendix A defines key terms, including constituency, security incident (any adverse event which compromises some aspect of computer or network security), vendor and vulnerability. To count as a CSIRT, a team must provide a secure channel for reports, help its constituency handle incidents and disseminate incident-related information.
sections.eli5: The memo includes a pretend filled-in form so teams can see what a finished one looks like. They can copy ideas, but they do not have to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is not directly about the security of protocols, applications or networks, nor about particular responses to incidents. It only concerns how CSIRTs describe their responses. Even so, teams must operate securely: they need secure communication channels with other teams and constituents, and must secure their own systems and infrastructure to protect their constituency and keep the identity of victims and reporters confidential.
sections.eli5: A team that keeps secrets must also keep its own locks strong, so the people who ask for help are not exposed.
